usage: 을 marks the object you look at
examples: There are many restaurants around the hotel.
Is there a cafe near the station?
I walked slowly around the area.
nuance: 주변 means the area or things around a spot, a bit wider than 근처 ('the vicinity'). Travelers use it constantly for 'around the hotel/station'. It is almost always followed by 에 (location) or used as N + 주변.
mistakes: Saying 주변 식당 without 에; for location say 주변에 식당이 있어요.
Confusing 주변 (the surrounding area) with 주말 (weekend) — they look similar but are unrelated.

examples: There is a convenience store at the end of the road.
길 끝에 = at the end of the road
Please stand at the very end of this line.
The trip is already at its end.
nuance: 끝 is the physical or time 'end/tip' of something. Note the spelling has the rare final consonant ㅌ, and it is pronounced 'kkeut'. It pairs naturally with 에 for a place ('at the end') and with 맨 for emphasis ('the very end').
mistakes: Mispronouncing or misspelling as 끋 or 끝ㅌ — the correct form is 끝 with a single final ㅌ.
Using the verb 끝나다 (to finish) when you only need the noun 끝 (the end).

examples: The restroom is over that way.
If you go this way, it's the exit.
nuance: 쪽 means a side or direction and is one of the most useful travel words for giving and asking directions. It attaches to 이/그/저/어느 and to 오른/왼 (오른쪽, 왼쪽). To say 'in that direction' use 쪽 + 으로.
mistakes: Writing 이 쪽 with a space; 이쪽, 저쪽, 오른쪽 are written as one word.
Saying 이쪽에 가요 for direction; use 이쪽으로 가요 (으로 = toward).

examples: I want to rest in a quiet place.
There are many places I want to visit.
가 보고 싶은 곳 = places I want to go
nuance: 곳 is a slightly more written or polite word for 'place' than 데. It often follows an adjective or a modifying clause (조용한 곳, 가 본 곳). For a location use 곳에서 (action there) or 곳에 (existence there).
mistakes: Pronouncing 곳 as 'got' fully; the final ㅅ becomes a 't' stop, so it sounds like 'got' without releasing the t.
Forgetting the particle: say 곳에서 쉬어요, not just 곳 쉬어요.

examples: I have no place to go.
갈 데 = a place to go
Do you know a quiet place?
Where is the spot that hurts?
아픈 데 = the place that hurts
nuance: 데 is a casual, everyday word for 'place' and must always follow a modifier (갈 데, 조용한 데) — it never stands alone like 곳 can. Travelers hear it a lot in speech: 갈 데, 먹을 데, 쉴 데. Do not confuse this noun 데 with the connector ~는데.
mistakes: Using 데 by itself (데가 있어요 X) — it needs a modifier in front: 갈 데가 있어요.
Mixing up the place-noun 데 with the sentence connector -는데 ('but/and').

usage: a spot to sit or be
examples: 자리로 주세요 = give me the seat
Is there an empty seat here?
I sat in my seat and waited.
자리에 앉다 = sit in a seat
nuance: 자리 is the everyday word for a seat or a spot to occupy — on a train, in a restaurant, at a theater. It is extremely useful for travel: 창가 자리 (window seat), 빈자리 (empty seat). Use 자리에 with 앉다 (to sit).
mistakes: Saying 의자 (a physical chair) when you mean 자리 (a seat/spot you reserve or take).
Forgetting 에 with 앉다: say 자리에 앉아요, not 자리 앉아요.

usage: an inside corner of a room/space
examples: My bag is in the corner of the room.
구석에 있어요 = is in the corner
I took a photo in the corner of the shop.
nuance: 구석 is an inside corner — where two walls of a room or space meet. It differs from 모퉁이, which is an outside corner of a street or building you turn at. Travelers use it for 'corner seat' or 'in the corner of the room'.
mistakes: Using 구석 for a street corner; for turning a street corner use 모퉁이.
Dropping the particle: say 구석에 있어요 (location) or 구석에서 (action there).

examples: My passport is inside the bag.
I found a coin inside my pocket.
The place in the photo is really pretty.
nuance: 속 means the inside or interior, often the deep inside of a 3D thing (bag, water, pocket) or a figurative inside (사진 속, 마음속). It overlaps with 안, but 속 stresses the substance/depth while 안 stresses being within boundaries. Use 속에 for location.
mistakes: Always swapping 속 and 안 — for a room or building 안 is more natural (방 안), while 속 fits filled or deep spaces (물속).
Forgetting 에: say 가방 속에 있어요, not 가방 속 있어요.

nuance: 바깥 means the outside or outdoors and is the natural opposite of 안 (inside). It is slightly more concrete than 밖, and the two are often interchangeable (바깥에 / 밖에). The final ㅌ links to following vowels, so 바깥에 sounds like 'ba-kka-te'.
mistakes: Misspelling as 바깟 or 바같 — the correct form ends in ㅌ: 바깥.
Confusing 바깥에 (outside, location) with 밖에 the particle meaning 'only' — context and a verb tell them apart.

examples: There are shops on both sides of the road.
People are standing on both sides of the door.
문 양쪽 = both sides of the door
nuance: 양쪽 combines 양 ('both') with 쪽 ('side') to mean 'both sides'. It is handy for describing a street, a door, or a choice between two options (양쪽 다 = both). For location, follow it with 에.
mistakes: Saying 둘쪽 — the correct word is 양쪽, not a number + 쪽.
Using 양쪽 for three or more things; for 'every side' use 사방 or list them.

examples: The hotel's location is really good.
I checked the location on the map.
I'll send you my current location.
nuance: 위치 is a slightly more formal noun for 'location/position', common in travel apps, maps, and reviews (위치가 좋다 = good location). Unlike 곳/데 (a place you go), 위치 is the abstract idea of where something sits. Pair it with 가 (description) or 를 (to check/send).
mistakes: Using 위치 when you mean a 'place to go' — for that use 곳 or 데, not 위치.
Mispronouncing 치 — 위치 is 'wi-chi', not 'wi-ti'.

examples: I have to go in the opposite direction.
nuance: 방향 means 'direction' in a broader, more abstract sense than 쪽. You use it when checking if you are heading the right way (방향이 맞아요?) or going the wrong way (반대 방향). For 'toward a direction', add 으로.
mistakes: Confusing 방향 (direction) with 방학 (school vacation) — they sound close but differ.
Saying 방향에 가요 for movement; use 방향으로 가요 (으로 = toward).

examples: There is a big door at the front of the building.
Let's meet in front of the station.
nuance: 정면 means the front face of something or the spot directly ahead — the front of a building, or 'straight in front of you'. It is more specific than 앞 (general 'front'): 정면 stresses the face that looks straight at you. Use 정면에 (location) or 정면으로 (direction).
mistakes: Using 정면 for casual 'in front of me'; everyday speech prefers 앞.
Forgetting the particle: 정면에 있어요 (location) or 정면으로 가요 (direction).

examples: I put the cup at the edge of the table.
I walked along the edge of the lake.
nuance: 가장자리 is the outer edge or rim of a flat thing — a table, a lake, a page. It differs from 끝 (the end/tip of something long) and 구석 (an inside corner). Travelers use it for walking along an edge or putting things near the rim. Use 가장자리에 for location.
mistakes: Using 가장자리 for the end of a road; that is 끝, not 가장자리.
Confusing 가장자리 (edge) with 가장 (most/-est) — 가장 is an unrelated adverb.
